client: I've been really stressed out lately about my grades and whether I'm going to keep my scholarship this term. Last semester I got a pretty bad grade on my final project, and it's been sitting in the back of my mind ever since, like this constant low hum of dread. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is just... real, you know? It's not in my head.
therapist: You're absolutely right that the pressure is real — scholarship requirements and grades carry genuine, concrete stakes, and I want you to know I'm not here to minimize any of that. At the same time, I'm curious about that "constant low hum of dread" you mentioned, because sometimes the way our minds *carry* a real stressor can add an extra layer of weight on top of the actual problem. I wonder — when that dread shows up, what kinds of thoughts tend to come with it?

client: Yeah, I mean... the thoughts are usually something like "what if I fail this exam and lose my scholarship and then disappoint everyone who believed in me." It kind of spirals from one bad grade to basically my whole future falling apart in like five seconds flat. And underneath all of that is this feeling that I don't really deserve to be here in the first place, like I just got lucky and eventually everyone's going to figure that out.
therapist: What you're describing — that lightning-fast spiral from one exam to your entire future, and that feeling of not truly belonging — is something many high-achieving people experience, and it even has a name: impostor phenomenon. It's worth gently noticing that the same mind telling you "you just got lucky" is the mind that *also* earned that scholarship in the first place, and those two things deserve to sit next to each other. What do you think someone who genuinely believed in you — one of those people you're afraid of disappointing — would say if they heard you describe yourself as just lucky?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to dismiss it as something you're just supposed to say to make me feel better. Like, even if my professor or my mom said "you earned this," I think I'd find a way to explain it away — maybe they don't see the full picture, or they're being kind. The idea that two opposite things can both be true at the same time, the luck and the earning, just feels like a contradiction I can't quite hold onto.
therapist: That instinct to explain away reassurance is actually really important information — it tells us that the belief "I don't deserve to be here" isn't really waiting for *evidence*, it's working more like a filter that lets doubt in and keeps confidence out. You're not failing to think clearly; you've just got a very well-practiced mental habit of protecting that belief from being challenged. I'm curious — can you think of one specific moment, maybe a piece of work or a decision you made, where you can trace a clear line between *your* effort or thinking and a good outcome, something that's harder to hand entirely to luck?

client: I mean... there was this project last quarter where my manager was completely checked out and I basically had to figure out the whole rollout plan myself. It actually went well — people said it went well — but my first instinct right now is to say "well, anyone could have done that" or "I just got lucky the stakeholders were easy to work with." I can hear myself doing the thing you just described, and it's kind of unsettling to catch it happening in real time like that.
therapist: That moment of catching yourself mid-dismissal is genuinely significant — that's not a small thing, that's you observing your own mind in action, which is exactly the kind of awareness that creates room for change. Notice that "anyone could have done that" conveniently erases the fact that your manager *didn't* do it, the other people in the room *didn't* do it — you were the one who stepped up and figured it out. What does it feel like, even just physically, to let that reality land for a moment without immediately explaining it away?

client: Okay, when you put it that way... I notice something kind of tight in my chest, like a mix of wanting to accept it and also this immediate urge to deflect again. It's uncomfortable, honestly, like I'm waiting for someone to point out the flaw in the logic, to remind me why I shouldn't feel good about it. I guess I'm not used to just... sitting with something positive without it feeling like I'm setting myself up to be wrong.
therapist: That discomfort you're feeling is actually a really healthy sign — it means you're bumping up against the edges of an old belief rather than just sliding past it, and that's where real shifts can begin to happen. The feeling of "setting yourself up to be wrong" makes a lot of sense if your mind has learned that confidence is dangerous, but I want to gently offer that sitting with something positive isn't the same as claiming you're perfect or invincible. What do you think it would mean for you — not for anyone else, just for you — if you allowed yourself to own that project success, even just a little?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it's that simple. But if I let myself own the success, I think I'd just be waiting for the moment someone figures out I didn't really deserve it — like I'd be handing them ammunition. It's easier to stay small and quiet about it than to stick my neck out and have it cut off.
therapist: That image of "staying small" as a form of protection is so vivid, and it makes complete sense as a strategy — if you never claim anything, there's nothing to take away. But I want to reflect something back gently: that strategy might be keeping you *safe* from an imagined threat while also being the very thing that feeds the feeling of not belonging, because you never get to fully inhabit your own accomplishments. I'm wondering — has staying small actually protected you from the dread, or has it mostly just kept the dread quieter while still always there?

client: I mean... when you put it that way, I have to admit the dread doesn't actually go away, it just kind of... hums in the background constantly. Like I'm always waiting for someone to figure out I don't really belong here, even when nothing bad is happening. But I guess I never really thought about the fact that shrinking myself might actually be making that feeling worse, not better — that's kind of uncomfortable to sit with.
therapist: That discomfort you're sitting with right now is actually really meaningful — you've just noticed that the thing you've been using to feel safer might be quietly sustaining the very fear you're trying to escape, and that's a genuinely important insight to arrive at on your own. The hum doesn't go away with shrinking because the belief underneath it never gets a chance to be tested or challenged — it just gets to keep running unchecked in the background. I'm curious: if staying small isn't actually buying you safety, just silence, what might it look like to experiment — even in one tiny, low-stakes way — with letting yourself take up just a little more space?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it — like, intellectually I can follow the logic. But when you ask what it would look like to take up more space, my mind just goes kind of blank and then immediately jumps to all the ways it could go wrong. Even something "tiny and low-stakes" doesn't feel that way to me, because there's this voice that says any crack in the wall is where everything starts to fall apart.
therapist: That "any crack in the wall" image is really telling — it suggests your mind has learned to treat the whole structure as fragile, where even small risks feel existentially dangerous rather than just mildly uncomfortable. But I want to gently offer that the wall metaphor might be working against you here, because what you're actually building toward isn't a wall that holds everything out, but more like a foundation that can hold *you* even when things don't go perfectly. I wonder — can you think of a time in the past where you took a small risk, something did go imperfectly, and yet you were still standing afterward?

client: I hear what you're saying about the foundation versus the wall, and part of me gets it intellectually, but it still feels a little too neat, like a reframe that sounds good in theory. As for a time things went imperfectly and I survived... I mean, yeah, there have been moments, but my mind immediately jumps to "that was different" or "you just got lucky that time." It's hard to let those examples actually mean something when the anxiety is telling me this situation is uniquely dangerous.
therapist: You've just done something really important — you've named the exact move your mind makes to quarantine any evidence that might challenge the anxiety, that "this time is different" thought is like an immune response that keeps the belief protected from anything that might weaken it. And you're right that the reframes can feel too neat, because words alone can't fully override something that lives in your body as much as your mind — which is actually why I'm less interested in convincing you and more interested in helping you *discover* something through small experience rather than logic. So I'm curious: not what you *should* do, but what feels like the absolute tiniest possible moment this week where you could let yourself be seen just a little — even something that feels almost too small to count?

client: I appreciate that you're not trying to talk me out of it with logic, because yeah, that never really lands. But when you ask about letting myself be seen... even something tiny feels loaded, because my brain immediately goes to "what's the point, they won't really get it anyway." I guess maybe... texting back my coworker who reached out last week, instead of leaving it on read like I have been — that feels small enough that I can't really justify avoiding it, but it still makes me nervous.
therapist: That example you just came up with yourself is perfect — not because it's risk-free, but because you found it on your own terms, which means some part of you already believes it might be worth doing. I also want to gently notice that "what's the point, they won't really get it" is worth holding lightly, because it might be another way the wall keeps itself intact by closing the door before anyone even gets a chance to surprise you. What do you imagine might happen — even in the best case — if you sent that text and your coworker actually did get it, even just a little?
